ahead.title: How the engine holds the game's state
ahead.decides: Where each fact of a running game lives and is decided, how a fact changes, how it is kept so that a restart loses nothing, and how every screen receives it and catches up after a reconnect. It also settles what each fact and each copy does when a game starts or ends, at a system reset, at a restart and at a pack change. It is the hardest decision to reverse, so it comes first.
ahead.drivers: The promises [[promise:J2]], [[promise:J5]], [[promise:J3]] and [[promise:J9]]. The quality targets [[qt:QT1]], [[qt:QT3]], [[qt:QT4]], [[qt:QT5]], [[qt:QT16]] and [[qt:QT17]]. The extension cases [[ex:EX2]], [[ex:EX8]] and [[ex:EX19]].
ahead.settled: The four words for the game's live facts stand ([[dec:four-words-for-the-game-s-live-facts]]): runtime state, authority, copy and delivery path, and an outside program can be an authority. They name the facts and decide nothing about how the engine holds them. Five of the nine questions the pass answers ([[dec:the-nine-questions-the-pass-answers]]) bear on this decision: “Who decides each fact”; “One question gets one answer”; “Each fact at a game boundary”; “How copies update and show their age”; “Reconnect snapshot built like live update”. Since the design rounds go by decision, the record reads the nine as checks on each design, a reading still to be confirmed with you. The night's record is written from the facts the engine decided and carries the pack the game ran and the texts the players saw ([[dec:the-night-s-record-and-the-after-game-article]]). Whatever is chosen shows up in the published protocol ([[dec:one-published-protocol-and-an-outside-test-bench]]). A lost connection or a device that goes down mid-game must not stop the game ([[dec:no-technical-failure-stops-a-game]]): how the game's state carries on through a failure, and how it comes back together afterwards, is part of this decision, with the fallbacks the GMs see.
ahead.panel: The panel proposes two or three ways of holding the state, blind, from the goal, the requirements and the setting; the design round then puts them side by side, each checked against the promises, the quality targets, the extension cases and the sixteen design flaws as test situations. The situations nearest this decision: [[flaw:C1]], [[flaw:C4]], [[flaw:C5]], [[flaw:C6]], [[flaw:C9]] and [[flaw:C11]]. The round also says how each design serves applying a change while the engine runs, between games, the separate trial copy of the engine, capturing the night (the roster, the notes, the photos), players' phones and standalone games, and how the game carries on when a tablet's connection, a device or the show machine fails. No option is proposed here.

ahead.title: The published protocol's form
ahead.decides: The protocol itself is decided; this decision settles its form. How each message and each file is defined and versioned, how a device's code is generated from the definition or checked against it, and what every fact and reply carries with it, such as how old it is and how sure the engine is. It also settles the version rules: what an older tablet, scanner or pack does when the engine is newer.
ahead.drivers: The promises [[promise:J10]], [[promise:J1]], [[promise:J7]] and [[promise:J3]]. The quality targets [[qt:QT18]], [[qt:QT22]], [[qt:QT19]], [[qt:QT4]], [[qt:QT7]], [[qt:QT31]], [[qt:QT32]], [[qt:QT35]] and [[qt:QT41]]. The extension cases [[ex:EX10]], [[ex:EX17]], [[ex:EX18]], [[ex:EX19]] and [[ex:EX21]].
ahead.settled: One published, versioned protocol defines everything that crosses the engine's edge, every program's code is generated from it or checked against it, and it is designed in an early design round, not merely collected ([[dec:one-published-protocol-and-an-outside-test-bench]]); the full explanation is under Decided directions below. The components keep their settled roles ([[dec:the-role-question-starts-from-settled-roles]]): the player scanners show token content and report scans, the GM scanner is the command center, the scoreboards show the public results. Two of the nine questions bear on it ([[dec:the-nine-questions-the-pass-answers]]): “Service state travels with its health” and “Each component gets what its role needs”. The night's record is one of the files the protocol defines, read by the Director Console from outside ([[dec:the-night-s-record-and-the-after-game-article]]). The record's reading that the protocol takes the place of the drafted message lists among the design half's handover documents ([[dec:five-documents-the-design-half-hands-over]]) is to be confirmed with you. How an extension made for all games relates to the engine's main release is your open question ([[dec:two-kinds-of-game-extension]]); the version rules this round settles are where that answer lands.
ahead.panel: The panel brings two or three forms side by side, checked against the requirements; the hardware scanner, whose program is written in another language, is the hard case every form must serve, and so is any other hardware a production brings later ([[dec:the-engine-is-hardware-flexible-the-roadmap-sets-the-bounds]]). The design flaws nearest this decision, as test situations: [[flaw:C7]], [[flaw:C13]], [[flaw:C14]], [[flaw:C2]] and [[flaw:C12]].

ahead.title: Where authority lives across devices, offline and standalone included
ahead.decides: For each fact, which device or program decides it: the engine in a networked game, the tablet in a standalone one, an outside program for what it alone knows. You decided that a lost connection must not stop the game ([[dec:no-technical-failure-stops-a-game]]). What a tablet does with a scan while its connection is down, and who wins when two tablets claimed one token while apart, is your question “A GM tablet cut off from the engine” on [[page:decisions]]; how a networked game carries on if the show machine itself fails, without becoming a mixed game ([[dec:standalone-games-declared-never-mixed]]), is your question “The show machine fails mid-game” there. This round designs whichever you choose. Where the fact “this game is standalone” is kept, and how it reaches every device.
ahead.drivers: The promises [[promise:J2]], [[promise:J3]], [[promise:J8]], [[promise:J9]] and [[promise:J5]]. The quality targets [[qt:QT3]], [[qt:QT7]], [[qt:QT31]], [[qt:QT37]], [[qt:QT38]], [[qt:QT39]], [[qt:QT40]] and [[qt:QT17]]. The extension cases [[ex:EX12]], [[ex:EX4]] and [[ex:EX10]].
ahead.settled: Standalone games are a capability of the engine for rooms where a network connection is not feasible, or where only GM scanners, player scanners (phone or hardware) or both are wanted; a game declares it, and no game mixes networked and standalone devices ([[dec:standalone-games-declared-never-mixed]]); where the declaration is held (the venue profile, the pack, the game's record or each device) is left to this round. An outside program can be an authority ([[dec:four-words-for-the-game-s-live-facts]]). The components keep their settled roles ([[dec:the-role-question-starts-from-settled-roles]]). The question “Who decides each fact” is the central one of the nine ([[dec:the-nine-questions-the-pass-answers]]). Your words “player scanners (phone or hardware)” answer the hardware scanner's standalone mode. Your open questions feeding this round: which shapes of standalone game the engine supports (GM scanners, player scanners or both; how many GM tablets), and how a networked game carries on if the show machine fails. The quality target “[[qt:QT3]]” says the game carries on while a tablet is disconnected and points what the tablet does meanwhile, and who wins a conflict, at your question “A GM tablet cut off from the engine”; this round builds your answer.
ahead.panel: The panel brings two or three placements of authority side by side, each tested against the requirements and against these situations: [[flaw:C9]], [[flaw:C1]], [[flaw:C7]], [[flaw:C13]] and the proposed seventeenth design flaw, [[flaw:N1]]. Each design must say who decides when there is no engine, and how the rules stay equal on the engine and on the tablet, with a test that proves it.

ahead.title: How games and venues extend the engine
ahead.decides: What a pack may declare and what a venue profile may declare, and where the engine leaves room for a developer to add a scoring model, a kind of screen, a device kind, a program it drives or a content source without touching the rest. Which of your two kinds of extension each change is ([[dec:two-kinds-of-game-extension]]): a mechanic the game's own maker builds inside the game from what the engine can already do, such as players changing the room's lighting by scanning tokens; or an ability a developer adds once for every game, such as a service for audio in several rooms. How far the game's maker may go with no developer (your question “What a game's maker may build inside the pack” on [[page:decisions]]), and where the second kind plugs in (your question “How an extension for all games reaches a production” there). Which settings are the engine's fixed requirements and which are a production's own, and where a production's settings live ([[dec:the-engine-says-what-is-fixed-and-what-each-production-sets]]). How the check at publish refuses a pack that contradicts itself or asks for something this engine lacks, naming what is at fault. Where settings that belong to no game live, such as whether the engine starts each program itself or uses one already running: in the venue profile or in a file of their own.
ahead.drivers: The promises [[promise:J1]], [[promise:J4]], [[promise:J8]] and [[promise:J6]]. The quality targets [[qt:QT9]], [[qt:QT10]], [[qt:QT12]], [[qt:QT20]], [[qt:QT21]], [[qt:QT22]], [[qt:QT23]], [[qt:QT24]] and [[qt:QT6]]. The extension cases [[ex:EX1]], [[ex:EX3]], [[ex:EX4]], [[ex:EX5]], [[ex:EX6]], [[ex:EX7]], [[ex:EX9]], [[ex:EX11]], [[ex:EX13]], [[ex:EX15]], [[ex:EX16]], [[ex:EX18]], [[ex:EX20]] and [[ex:EX22]].
ahead.settled: The pack, the venue profile, the night's record and the media list are among the files the published protocol defines ([[dec:one-published-protocol-and-an-outside-test-bench]]); for an open-source platform, the protocol and the pack format are what other people build against. The standing rules on [[page:requirements]] hold: the engine holds no opinion about game design, media never lives inside the pack, and nothing in the engine assumes one kit, one pack or one production. Whether paper documents join the pack, with “unlocked” recorded during play, waits for this round ([[dec:the-night-s-record-and-the-after-game-article]]). The pieces of the hardening block already built into the engine (the kinds of equipment a pack can ask for and a venue profile can name, the code that marks equipment not installed tonight, and the smallest test set-up) stay in the engine and change only where a design choice requires ([[dec:corrections-to-the-readers-and-the-hardening-pieces]]). You named two kinds of game extension and keep them apart ([[dec:two-kinds-of-game-extension]]); your wording is tentative and the record keeps it so. Two of your questions stay open there: how an extension for all games relates to the engine's main release, and which piece each kind changes (the pack, the engine's code, an added outside service). The engine stays agnostic about any one production's numbers and says what is fixed and what each production sets ([[dec:the-engine-says-what-is-fixed-and-what-each-production-sets]]); ALN's numbers are the first set, a call of the agent running the pass that you can overrule on [[page:decisions]]. The promises are offered for review on [[page:decisions]]; the panel designs against them as you leave them.
ahead.panel: The panel brings two or three ways of extending side by side: what the pack declares, what the profile declares, and the places a developer adds to. Each is tested against the extension cases above, with the toy game, the second game's four needs (two-tap actions, hidden facts that spread, a score read off a graph, a constellation screen) and your two examples (players changing the lighting by scanning tokens, made inside a game; audio in several rooms, added for every game) as the working examples, and against these situations: [[flaw:C12]], [[flaw:C15]], [[flaw:C3]], [[flaw:C10]] and [[flaw:N1]].

ahead.title: How one engine runs as many separate copies
ahead.decides: How the show's copy of the engine, a trial copy, a test copy and a second kit's copy each keep their own files, network ports, settings, programs and passes, so that none can stop another's programs, read its records or accept its passes. How the engine tells its own program from a stranger's copy of the same program on the same machine. What is set per copy and per kit, such as the kit's network name. Where the designer's trial copy runs, a laptop or the show machine between games, is open.
ahead.drivers: The promises [[promise:J6]], [[promise:J10]] and [[promise:J8]]. The quality targets [[qt:QT11]], [[qt:QT27]], [[qt:QT43]], [[qt:QT24]], [[qt:QT23]] and [[qt:QT36]]. The extension cases [[ex:EX14]], [[ex:EX16]], [[ex:EX21]] and [[ex:EX23]].
ahead.settled: The question “Only the live engine touches the show” asks whether anything other than the live engine, tests today and the trial copy later, can touch the live show ([[dec:the-nine-questions-the-pass-answers]]). The tests become a test bench outside the engine ([[dec:one-published-protocol-and-an-outside-test-bench]]), and the test rig is built at the start of building as part of that bench, where a thin first version of the new design runs end to end ([[dec:build-the-test-rig-when-building-starts]]); both need copies of the engine that stay separate. How a standalone tablet runs its game, with the same parts the engine runs or an engine of its own, is still open (see Later choices). The engine is meant to be flexible about hardware, within the bounds the current roadmap sets ([[dec:the-engine-is-hardware-flexible-the-roadmap-sets-the-bounds]]), so a copy on a different machine is one of the cases this round keeps in view.
ahead.panel: The panel brings two or three ways of keeping copies apart, tested against the requirements and against these situations: [[flaw:C8]], [[flaw:C5]] and [[flaw:C15]]. Each design says what a copy owns, what a kit owns and what the machine owns, and how a test run on the show machine during a show is kept from the show.

ahead.title: How today's engine moves to the new design
ahead.decides: Whether today's engine is changed in place, area by area, a new engine is built beside it and the pieces swapped over, or a mix of the two. Either way the build half starts with a thin first version of the new design. How the game keeps running on blue, the show machine in use now, while the new engine is built for green, the new machine this work builds. What the move does with today's tests and with the hardening pieces already built. This decision feeds the build plan, which follows the design rounds.
ahead.drivers: The promises [[promise:J10]] and [[promise:J5]]. The quality targets [[qt:QT41]], [[qt:QT42]], [[qt:QT26]] and [[qt:QT19]]. The extension case [[ex:EX17]].
ahead.settled: The build half changes the engine to follow the design, one area at a time, as the first work in the new roadmap, and starts with a thin first version of the new design running end to end on a new test bench ([[dec:one-program-design-half-then-build-half]]); each area gets its detailed design just before it is built. The game keeps running on blue until the new engine is ready to swap in on green, and no date governs the work ([[dec:the-architecture-pass-is-the-work-now]]). The test rig is built when building starts, not to reproduce today's problems first; if this decision chooses to change today's engine in place, pinning down today's behaviour first comes back ([[dec:build-the-test-rig-when-building-starts]]). The pieces of the hardening block already built stay in the engine ([[dec:corrections-to-the-readers-and-the-hardening-pieces]]), and the truth sweep's purpose, proving that every screen tells the truth, moves into the build work ([[dec:the-truth-sweep-s-charter-is-retired]]). Whether each build area still starts with its test failing on today's engine is read as overtaken unless the move changes the engine in place; that reading is to be confirmed with you ([[dec:one-program-design-half-then-build-half]]).
ahead.panel: The panel brings two or three ways of moving side by side, each priced by what it needs from today's engine, with [[page:today]] as the evidence of what already works and what is already well built. The situations nearest this decision: [[flaw:C15]], [[flaw:C16]] and [[flaw:C5]]. The round ends by handing the build plan its starting point; the build plan settles the order of the work.

panel.title: The panel's brief
intro: Before the first design round, an independent panel of three architects proposes the top-level design ([[dec:independent-architects-propose-the-top-level-design]]). You said the context the panel gets is critical, so its brief comes to you before it runs. It follows [[dec:what-the-architects-panel-sees-and-when]]. Of the choices that decision leaves open, one is yours: what the blind round gets, on [[page:decisions]]. The lenses and whether the second round reads today's code are calls of the agent running the pass, listed there with their reasons for you to overrule. The brief was revised on 2026-11-02 for your decisions of that day. The panel runs only after you review the requirements and approve this brief.

sections.title: Who is on the panel
paragraphs: Three architects. Each is a fresh AI agent on the strongest model available. None has seen the conversations or the planning documents of the agent running the pass, and none sees another's work until the second round. Each has one lens, so that the three proposals differ. A lens says where an architect looks hardest; every architect still answers to every requirement.

items.lead: State, authority and keeping the game going through a failure
items.text: How a live game's facts are held, changed, ordered and recovered across the show machine, the tablets, the phones and the hardware scanners, on a network that drops, with standalone games included; and how the game carries on, and the GMs know their fallbacks, when a connection, a device or the show machine fails ([[dec:no-technical-failure-stops-a-game]]).

How designers, venue technicians and outside developers extend the platform: games as packs, venues as profiles, the two kinds of game extension (a mechanic the game's maker builds from what the engine can already do, inside the game; an ability a developer adds once for every game), new kinds of screen, device, hardware and outside program, the published protocol as what other people build against, and what is fixed and what each production sets ([[dec:two-kinds-of-game-extension]], [[dec:the-engine-is-hardware-flexible-the-roadmap-sets-the-bounds]], [[dec:the-engine-says-what-is-fixed-and-what-each-production-sets]]).

How one owner and AI agents keep the engine easy to understand, change, test and release for years: how small and clear each piece is, and how a change is made, tested on the test bench and shipped with no risk to a show.

sections.title: The blind round
paragraphs: Each architect gets one prepared folder and nothing else:

items.text: In your words: “design a long-term optimal architecture for our engine that makes it intuitive and easy to maintain, continue development on, and extend”.

As you leave them after review on [[page:requirements]]: the ten promises; the quality targets, each number sorted as the engine's requirement or limit, a production's setting (ALN's given as the first set) or a technical default, a sorting the agent running the pass made and marked as its own; the extension cases, each marked as one of the two kinds of extension or neither; and the standing rules.

ALN's kit is the first production's hardware, given as facts, not as the engine's requirements ([[dec:the-engine-is-hardware-flexible-the-roadmap-sets-the-bounds]]). ALN's show is one game of about two hours at one venue, with a few dozen devices. ALN's show machine is one Raspberry Pi 5 that drives the TV over HDMI and the room's sound and must go from power-on to a running show with no technician. The engine drives the room's outside programs (video, music, sound with Bluetooth speakers, the venue's lighting), and any of them can crash or be missing. ALN's devices are GM tablets (Android tablets running Chrome, for staff only, sometimes offline), players' own phones (a web page, with no install and no accounts), hardware scanners (small boards with an NFC reader, a small screen, an SD card and Wi-Fi, whose firmware is updated by cable) and NFC tokens. The venue's Wi-Fi can drop at any moment, and no internet is assumed. A game's content is written in Notion today and exported into the pack; its large media files live beside the pack. The mature engine is meant to be flexible about hardware; the current roadmap sets the bounds, and the architects may propose where. Another production may bring a different game, venue and kit, and must be able to find what is fixed and what it may set ([[dec:the-engine-says-what-is-fixed-and-what-each-production-sets]]). One owner, who is not an engineer, develops the engine with AI agents, so every piece must be easy for an agent to read and change safely; a future open-source community, and other productions, may join.

items.lead: Your decisions that bind any design
items.text: [[dec:one-published-protocol-and-an-outside-test-bench]]; [[dec:standalone-games-declared-never-mixed]], with its purpose in your words; [[dec:four-words-for-the-game-s-live-facts]]; [[dec:the-night-s-record-and-the-after-game-article]]; [[dec:the-role-question-starts-from-settled-roles]]; and your four decisions of 2026-11-02: [[dec:no-technical-failure-stops-a-game]], [[dec:the-engine-is-hardware-flexible-the-roadmap-sets-the-bounds]], [[dec:two-kinds-of-game-extension]] and [[dec:the-engine-says-what-is-fixed-and-what-each-production-sets]]; if you agree (your question on what the blind round gets, on [[page:decisions]]). The panel gets your words and the open questions, never the agent's readings of your words that the record marks to be confirmed; the requirements it gets state only what you settled and name the open questions. The one reading that reaches it, the sorting of the numbers, is marked in the requirements as the agent's call.

items.lead: The six decisions ahead, as the agenda
items.text: If you agree (your question on what the blind round gets, on [[page:decisions]]). An architect may add, split or merge decisions and must say why. How today's engine moves to the new design waits for the second round, when today's engine is known.

after: Each architect writes a top-level design, decision by decision: the choice; one or two alternatives they rejected, with the cost of each; a table of how the design keeps each promise, meets each quality target and allows each extension case, naming any it cannot meet; for each kind of failure mid-show (a tablet's connection, a device, the show machine, an outside program), what the GMs can still do and how the game carries on; its riskiest assumption; and the trial run, a throwaway prototype, that would test that assumption fastest.

sections.title: The second round: meeting today's engine
paragraphs: After the blind round, each architect also gets:

items.text: A fact sheet of what runs where, in what language, and what works today; and the code with its component guides, to read but not change. Reading the code is a call of the agent running the pass, listed on [[page:decisions]] for you to overrule.

items.lead: The sixteen design flaws, as test situations
items.text: What goes wrong at a show, the problems behind it and where in today's code they sit, with no fix attached.

items.lead: The other two proposals, and the earlier candidate
items.text: The 17-part design drawn bottom-up from today's engine, as one more proposal.

after: Each architect tests every proposal (their own, the other two and the earlier candidate) against the sixteen situations and today's facts: which situations it removes, which it leaves, and what moving today's engine to it would cost. They critique the others, then revise their own design and say what changed and why. The second round also gives the last decision ahead its real options: rebuild beside today's engine, change it in place piece by piece, or a mix.

sections.title: The synthesis
paragraphs: One more agent, who proposed nothing, reads all of it and writes, for each decision ahead: the options the panel found, their costs, where the architects agreed and where they did not, the trial runs worth doing before choosing, and the questions only you can answer. A checker reads the synthesis against the proposals and corrects anything it misstates or leaves out. The synthesis becomes the agenda of the first design round, and a page on this site. The six proposals, three from each round, stay in the repository in full.

sections.title: What is withheld, and how
paragraphs: Withheld from the blind round: the recommendations and leading guesses of the agent running the pass, among them its readings of your words of 2026-11-02 that the record marks to be confirmed; the earlier candidate, which enters the second round as one more proposal; the earlier lists of design choices; today's engine and its review. Withheld from both rounds: the reasoning of the agent running the pass, the review's conclusions about fixes, and the earlier candidate's table of alternatives.

A script builds each round's folder from the sources (the requirements files, the standing rules, the decision record). Each architect is told to read only its folder, plus the code in the second round, and never the planning documents. Nothing technical stops an agent from opening a file it was told to leave alone, so the synthesis's checker also looks for traces of withheld material in every proposal.

sections.title: Size and cost
paragraphs: About eight agents: three in the blind round, three in the second round, the synthesis and its checker. It takes two to three hours and several million tokens of AI use, about as much as one of the larger runs that built this site.

decided.title: The published protocol
paragraphs: The published protocol is one written definition of everything that crosses the engine's edge, kept in one place with a version number. It defines what a device may ask (“this team turns in this token”, “start the game”, “play this video”); what the engine answers (done; refused, and why; held for later; try again); what the engine tells screens (the scores, the clock, what is playing, each service's health, each with how old and how sure it is); and the files that carry a game or a night (the pack, the venue profile, the night's record, the list of media files).

The code on every side is generated from that one definition or checked against it: the engine, the GM tablet, the phone, the TV and the design tool; the hardware scanner gets its names and its test examples from it. A change starts in the definition. Anything that no longer matches fails when the code is built, not during a show. Version rules say what an older tablet, scanner or pack does when the engine is newer.

It is the line between the engine's inside and everything around it. Inside, the design can be reorganised freely as long as the protocol holds. Outside, everything relies on it: your devices and games, the tools, a future developer, and the Director Console reading the night's record. For an open-source platform, it and the pack format are what other people build against. The other big decisions show up in it. For example, if facts are numbered in order, a reconnecting screen asks for everything after a given number; and if a game is standalone, the tablet speaks the same protocol to whatever runs the game on it. That is why it comes early in the design rounds.

Today the repository has written lists of what crosses the edge: the engine's written lists of web requests, live messages and the night's record, the venue profile's format and the pack formats, checked by a few tests, while every program copies the names by hand. The protocol consolidates and standardizes them, becomes the source of the code, and is designed rather than only collected.
It is not a program that runs. It does not replace the outside programs' own protocols: the video player, the music player and the lighting system keep theirs, and the engine adapts to them inside.

Its cost: generating code for the engine and the web programs, which share one language, and in part for the hardware scanner's program in its own; a version policy; and the discipline that every change starts in the definition. Together with the test bench it replaces the earlier candidate's part [[part:P16]] ([[dec:one-published-protocol-and-an-outside-test-bench]]). Its form is the decision ahead on the protocol's form, above.

decided.title: The test bench outside the engine
paragraphs: The tests move to a test bench outside the engine ([[dec:one-published-protocol-and-an-outside-test-bench]]). A test is the engine running with a stand-in venue profile: a profile that binds the pack's names to software stand-ins for video, sound, lights and speakers, which can be generated from the pack's own needs so that every need is met. On the bench a developer runs a whole game end to end on a laptop or a cloud machine with no venue hardware: the engine, the GM tablet's app, both player scanners' software and the TV page.

The same engine, the same pack and the same checks run at every test level (logic only; real programs with stand-in hardware; the home test bed; the venue), and each run records which checks it could not do and why. Every change runs the full set of tests twice, once with ALN's pack and once with the toy game's; a test that cannot run on this machine fails loudly with its reason; every test stand-in is compared with the real thing it stands for. A test run on the show machine keeps its own files, network ports and settings, and cannot stop a program it did not start.

“Proof” stays a quality every part must meet: a passing test run means the show works for two games, and no test reaches a live show. The newcomer's first demo, the designer's try-my-change loop and the developer's test bench are one kind of rehearsal at different depths. The build half starts with a thin first version of the new design running end to end on this bench ([[dec:one-program-design-half-then-build-half]]).

decided.title: The test rig built when building starts
paragraphs: The test rig is an automated machine that runs the real engine with the real video, music, audio and lighting programs and stand-ins for the room's equipment, so a design flaw can be made to happen for real instead of being read off the code. It was lost when the cloud computer it ran on was wiped.

It no longer comes before design ([[dec:build-the-test-rig-when-building-starts]]). It is built at the start of building, as part of the new test bench where the thin first version of the new design runs end to end, not to reproduce today's problems first. It had come before the design rounds, right after the review that named the design flaws, meant to reproduce four findings before design (the deleted token still refused, the music panel behind live music, the ended game returning after a restart, the reset that leaves music out), situations under [[flaw:C1]], [[flaw:C2]], [[flaw:C4]] and [[flaw:C5]]. The question of how much the rig proves before design is withdrawn.

Exception: if the decision on how today's engine moves to the new design chooses to change it in place, pinning down today's behaviour first comes back. The record reads two earlier conditions as overtaken by this decision, that each build area starts with its test failing on today's engine ([[dec:one-program-design-half-then-build-half]]) and that the rig reproduces each finding marked to be shown happening live before the design half ends ([[dec:when-the-design-half-is-finished]]); both readings are to be confirmed with you.

decided.title: The after-game boundary
paragraphs: What the players receive after the show, and their contact details, are the game's business, outside the engine; the engine's record is designed so the game's own tools can read it ([[dec:the-night-s-record-and-the-after-game-article]]). The second half of the promise “[[promise:J3]]” names the director and the players after the show. The engine makes the players no promise of their own for what they receive after the show.

The night's record carries the pack the game ran and the texts the players saw, so the article quotes what they held. Players' emails stay outside the engine; later, the game's own tools could collect them from the ticketing service. The Director Console stays a separate program, for now, that reads the engine's record; the record is designed so the console can later become ALN's own part of the engine's Review stage.

The two clocks (a sale is stamped with the tablet's time, a score adjustment with the engine computer's) join [[flaw:C9]] as a finding. Whether paper documents join the pack, with “unlocked” recorded during play, was not answered and waits for the design rounds.

decided.title: No technical failure stops a game
paragraphs: A lost connection or a device that goes down mid-game must not stop the game ([[dec:no-technical-failure-stops-a-game]]). At that moment the GMs must know the fallbacks that keep it running, with as little effect on the players as possible. In your words: “For more or less all use cases, having to pause a game because a connection was lost or a device goes down mid-game is the worst possible scenario.”

Two readings follow, which the record marks to be confirmed by you. First, a GM tablet that loses the engine keeps taking scans and the game carries on, rather than refusing scans until the connection returns; the quality target “[[qt:QT3]]” says the game carries on and leaves what the tablet does meanwhile to your question “A GM tablet cut off from the engine” on [[page:decisions]]. Second, the design must say how a networked game carries on if the show machine itself fails; that meets [[dec:standalone-games-declared-never-mixed]], and whether a game may carry on with its devices alone, and how the results come back together, is your question “The show machine fails mid-game” there. The new quality target “[[qt:QT44]]” is the test.

decided.title: The engine is hardware-flexible; the roadmap sets the bounds
paragraphs: The hardware is fixed only in that ALN runs on the kit you have bought ([[dec:the-engine-is-hardware-flexible-the-roadmap-sets-the-bounds]]). The mature engine is meant to be flexible about hardware, so the fundamental architecture must allow that flexibility later. The current roadmap sets realistic bounds: which flexibility it builds now, and where it names specific hardware requirements. Where the roadmap draws that line is open, for the design rounds and the build plan; the extension case “[[ex:EX28]]” carries it, and the panel's setting gives ALN's kit as the first production's hardware, not as the engine's requirement.

decided.title: Two kinds of game extension
paragraphs: A game can be extended in two ways, and the design keeps them apart ([[dec:two-kinds-of-game-extension]]). In the first, a new mechanic is built from what the engine can already do: a new action for the players, or a new way for the game to respond to triggers the engine already has. The game's own maker builds it, inside the game; in the long term it may be shared with other game makers. Your example: players change the room's lighting by scanning different tokens on a player scanner (“[[ex:EX25]]”). In the second, the engine cannot give the response yet, so a developer extends it for any game to use. Your example: a service such as Snapcast for audio in several rooms, so that areas get different soundtracks and the GMs can play a cue on every speaker or on chosen ones (“[[ex:EX26]]”).

Your wording is tentative (“should probably”, “probably”), and the record keeps it so. Two questions stay open as you named them: how an extension made for all games relates to the engine's main release, and which piece each kind changes (packs, the engine's code, added outside services). Both are your questions on [[page:decisions]]: “How an extension for all games reaches a production” and “What a game's maker may build inside the pack”. The round on how games and venues extend the engine, with the protocol's form, builds your answers.

decided.title: The engine says what is fixed and what each production sets
paragraphs: The engine is meant to serve many games in many production settings, so it stays agnostic about any one production's numbers: the devices and phones in a kit, the time from power-on to a running show, set-up time, how long records are kept, and the like ([[dec:the-engine-says-what-is-fixed-and-what-each-production-sets]]). Someone adopting the engine needs to know which requirements are fixed and which the engine lets them set, so they can fit it to their needs and their venue. ALN is one production: one game, one venue, the hardware you bought. Your next game may share them; the next person to use the engine may not.

Read from this, and the agent's call for you to overrule: the quality targets' numbers are sorted into the engine's fixed requirements and limits, each production's own settings with ALN's as the first set, and a few technical defaults. The sorting is on [[page:decisions]] with the targets; the extension case “[[ex:EX27]]” is the test for another production.

later.text: Where “this game is standalone” is declared: the venue profile (the earlier candidate favours it), the pack, the game's record or each device. It is decided in the round on where authority lives.
Getting facts onto screens: one delivery part for every fact, or the parts behind each promise delivering their own facts in one shared format.
The life of a game: one lifecycle part that alone moves the game and resets every part, or a table each part reads and applies itself.
The game rules as one shared body of code that the engine and the tablet both run, or two bodies kept equal by tests.
The equipment's interface: one per kind of thing the room can do (play a video, light a scene), or one per outside program.
The standalone tablet: the same record and lifecycle parts the engine runs, or an engine of its own.

How the fallback you choose under “The show machine fails mid-game” is built: how a networked game's state carries on without the show machine and comes back together afterwards, inside the rounds on how the engine holds the game's state and where authority lives; whatever is built must not make a mixed game by accident ([[dec:standalone-games-declared-never-mixed]]).
The scoreboard: one page shown in two places, the TV's browser and the Pi 4, or a view inside the GM app.
The config tool, the designer's and venue technician's tool: a separate program that talks to the engine only by sending it requests, never by writing its files, or pages the engine itself serves.
When a changed pack may be loaded while the engine runs. That is not built yet; the roadmap allows it only before a game starts or after it ends.

Where the setting lives that says whether the engine starts each outside program or uses one already running: in the venue technician's profile, as the earlier candidate has it, or in a file of its own, as the list of planned capabilities drawn from the roadmap has it. It is decided in the round on how games and venues extend the engine.

Where a production's own settings live (its kit's devices and phones, how long it keeps records): in the venue profile, in per-kit settings, or in both; and where the build plan places your answer to “Which hardware the first new engine requires, and what it must allow replacing” in the roadmap, as the hardware it names as a requirement and the hardware it leaves flexible. The first is decided in the round on how games and venues extend the engine; the second by the build plan ([[dec:the-engine-is-hardware-flexible-the-roadmap-sets-the-bounds]], [[dec:the-engine-says-what-is-fixed-and-what-each-production-sets]]).

The order of the work: by part (the earlier candidate put [[part:P13]] and [[part:P6]] first) or by block as the roadmap has it. The build plan, which starts with a thin first version, settles it after the design rounds.

Whether paper documents join the pack, with “unlocked” recorded during play, so the night's record can say which documents the players opened. Today the director marks them by hand after the show. It is decided in the round on how games and venues extend the engine.

How your answers to “How an extension for all games reaches a production” and “What a game's maker may build inside the pack” are built: the pack's format for what a maker declares, the places an add-on plugs into, and which piece each kind of extension changes in the design (the pack, the engine's code, an added outside service) ([[dec:two-kinds-of-game-extension]]), in the round on how games and venues extend the engine, with the protocol's form.

earlierNote: An earlier candidate, drawn bottom-up from today's engine: seventeen parts, how they would run on each device, and where a real alternative exists. It is one input among the panel's; the panel compares it with its own proposals in its second round, after proposing blind. Its part [[part:P16]] is replaced by the published protocol and the test bench ([[dec:one-published-protocol-and-an-outside-test-bench]]); nothing else in it is decided.
